column2: Hari alone is the supreme kinsman, Hari alone the highest goal; therefore Hari alone is to be worshipped, since he is the cause of consciousness.
Of the one to be worshipped — giver of heaven and liberation, ever blissful, faultless — O best of sages, supreme good will come.
Vishnu, pleased in heart, grants all desires to those who worship Hari without desire and with pure minds.
One who attentively hears or reads this obtains the fruit of the horse-sacrifice, O best of sages.
Thus the fruit of worshipping Hari has been told to you, O Brahmin; in brief and in detail — what else shall I tell you?
Therefore I speak only for the good of all people: Kali never troubles mortals devoted to Hari's name.
Hari's name, only the name, only the name is my life; in the Kali age there is no other way, none, none.
Suta said: Thus instructed by Sanaka, O Brahmins, Narada attained supreme peace and spoke again:
Narada said: "Lord, knower of all scriptures, by your great compassion you have revealed the light of the world, the supreme eternal Brahman.
This alone is supreme merit, this alone supreme austerity: to remember the lotus-eyed one who destroys all sin.
O Brahmin, this manifold world is made manifest by one consciousness; how can I understand what you said without an example?
Therefore tell me how Brahman is understood by one who is taught, so that my wavering mind may find stability."
Hearing the words of the great-souled Narada, O Brahmins, Sanaka, remembering the supreme Narayana, replied:
Sanaka said: "Brahmin, I wish to be devoted to meditation; ask Sanandana as you wish. He is skilled in the Vedanta scripture and, honoured by the highest, will remove your doubt."
Hearing Sanaka's words, Narada began to ask Sanandana about the dharmas of liberation.
Skin, flesh, bones, marrow and sinew as the fifth: this is the aggregate here in the body made of earth.
Energy, fire, anger, the eye and warmth, and what fire produces — these five are of fire in embodied beings.
Ear, nose, mouth, heart and abdomen: from space, these five elements are in the bodies of beings.
Phlegm, bile, sweat, fat and blood: these five of water are always in the bodies of beings.
From prana the creature is nourished; by vyana it sustains.
Apana goes downward; samana stays in the middle; by udana one breathes up. The five are described by their differences. These five winds envelop the embodied being.
The embodied one knows from earth the quality of smell, and from water taste. I shall tell you at length the qualities of smell.
Pleasant and unpleasant smell, sweet, pungent, far-spreading, compact, oily, dry and clear:
thus the extent of the earthly smell is to be known as ninefold. Light sees through the eyes, and touch is known through wind.
Sound, touch, form and taste are called qualities. I shall tell you of the knowledge of taste; hear it from me.
Taste is said by the sages of renowned minds to be of many kinds: sweet, salty, bitter, astringent, sour and pungent.
This is the sixfold extent of taste, held to belong to water. Sound, touch and form are called the three qualities of light.
Light sees forms, and form is said to be of many kinds: short, long, thick, four-sided, subtle and round;
white, black, red, blue, yellow, dawn-red; hard, smooth, fine, slimy, soft and rough.
Thus the qualities of light are held to be sixteenfold. Of these, space has one quality, called sound.
I shall tell the manifold extent of that sound: shadja, rishabha, gandhara, madhyama, dhaivata,
panchama, and nishada: thus the quality born of space is said to be sevenfold.
By power it is present everywhere, in water and the rest, in the sounds of drum, kettledrum, conch, thunder and chariot.
Thus sound born of space has many forms. The quality of wind is touch, and touch is held to be of many kinds:
hot, cold, pleasant, painful, oily, clear, rough, soft, smooth, light and heavy.
Sound and touch are known as the two qualities of wind; thus the quality of wind is said to be elevenfold.
They say sound is born of space; with these qualities of wind, he is conscious in unobstructed ways, and the course is uneven.
These elements are always nourished by those elements; water, fire and wind are always awake in bodies.
These are the root of the body, pervading the breaths here; having reached the earthly element, the strong one acts.
Fire, resting at the head, sustains the body; prana, abiding in the head and in fire, moves.
That creature, the Self of all beings, is the eternal Person; he is mind, intellect, ego, the elements and the object.
Thus here everywhere he is sustained by the breaths; at the back by samana, each resting in its own course.
Resting at the base of the bladder and the anus and in fire, apana moves, carrying urine and faeces.
The one that acts in effort and in regulated action, in three places, those who know spiritual knowledge call udana.
The wind lodged in all joints, in the bodies of men, is taught as vyana.
Fire spreads in the arms, impelled by samana; moving juices, water and faults, it acts excessively.
Between apana and prana, impelled by prana and apana, the fire together with the seat properly digests.
Up to the end of the anus, called the final part, from it semen arises, and all the channels of embodied beings.
From the meeting of the breaths, a meeting arises; the heat, to be known as fire, cooks the food of embodied beings.
Prana, carrying the force of fire, is struck back at the end of the anus; coming up again, it kindles the fire.
The stomach below the navel is the receptacle of the digested; above it, the receptacle of the undigested. At the root of the navel all the breaths are established.
All proceed from the heart, sideways, upward and downward; the channels, impelled by the ten breaths, carry the juices of food.
This is also the path of yogis by which they go to that state: with fatigue conquered, steady and wise, they place the Self in the head.
Thus in all embodied beings, with prana and apana arranged, in it fire is always kindled, like fire placed in a pot.
Others wish for honour even in animal wombs; others, with life exhausted, perish on the earth.
Addicted to devouring one another, full of greed and delusion, they revolve right here and do not go to the northern direction.
Those who, disciplined as students, serve their teachers — the wise know the road of all the worlds.
Thus this dharma, concisely told by me, was made by Brahma. He is wise who knows the world's dharma and adharma.
Bharadvaja said: "That which is thought of here as the 'adhyatma' of a person — what is adhyatma and how is it? Tell me, rich in austerity."
Bhrigu said: "O sage, what you ask as 'adhyatma' I shall explain to you, dear, the most beneficial happiness.
Connected with creation and dissolution, as shown by the teachers: knowing it, a person in the world gains joy and happiness,
and gains the fruit, and it is for the good of all beings. Earth, wind, space, water and fire as the fifth —
these great elements are the origin and dissolution of all beings. From where they were created, there they go again to dissolution.
The great elements, from beings, as the waves of the sea, or as a tortoise stretches out its limbs and draws them in again;
so the Self of beings withdraws the created beings again. The five great elements alone, in all beings, the maker of beings...
made in them well, yet the soul does not see him. Sound, ear and the openings — the three are born of space.
Touch, motion and skin are held to be the triad of wind. Form, eye and digestion are called the threefold fire.
Tastes, moisture and tongue are held to be the three qualities of water; smell, nose and body are the three qualities of earth.
The great elements are five, the sixth is called mind. The senses and mind are known to this one, O Bharata.
The seventh, they say, is the intellect; the eighth is the knower of the field. The ear is for hearing, the skin for touching,
the tongue for taking in taste, the nose for smell, the eye for seeing; the mind creates doubt,
the intellect for determination; the knower of the field stands as a witness. What sees upward, with the soles of the feet, downward and sideways —
by this all the inner space is pervaded by the all-pervading. By people the senses here are to be known in full.
Tamas, rajas and sattva — those states too rest on it. Understanding this intellect, a man, realizing the course of beings' coming and going,
reflecting slowly, gains the highest peace. Intellect is destroyed by the qualities, and from intellect the senses also.
The elements with mind as the sixth: where are qualities when the intellect is absent? Thus all this, moving and unmoving, is made of that.
It dissolves and arises; therefore it is thus indicated. By which one sees, that is the eye; by which one hears, the ear.
By which one smells, the nose they say; by the tongue one knows taste; by the skin one feels touch; the intellect changes at once.
By which one wishes for something, at that time it is the mind. From the support of the intellect, five separate objects arise in fivefold way;
they are called the senses; the unseen one presides over them. Intellect stays in the person and acts in three states.
Sometimes it gains delight, sometimes grieves, and sometimes it is neither in pleasure nor in pain.
Thus in men's minds it acts in three states. This intellect, made of states, rises above these three states.
As the sea is the lord of rivers and the ocean of its shores, the intellect, gone beyond the states, acts in the mind with the states.
The sage who thus abides follows his own nature. It always sets all the senses in motion.
Delight is sattva; grief is rajas; anger is tamas — these three. Whatever states are in this world, all are in these three.
Thus all the states residing in the intellect have been explained to you. The senses must all be conquered by the wise.
Sattva, rajas and tamas always reside in beings; the threefold feeling is seen in all creatures.
It is sattvic, rajasic and tamasic, O honourer. Pleasant touch is the quality of sattva; painful touch is the quality of rajas.
Joined with the quality of tamas, they become worldly. What is accompanied by delight, in body or mind,
and acts as a sattvic state — so one should say. What is joined with pain and brings displeasure to the self,
arising in action, know it as rajas, O best of sages. And what is joined with delusion, unmanifest and uneven,
unreasonable and unknowable, take it to be tamas. Joy, delight, bliss, happiness or tranquillity of mind,
whenever these arise somehow, they are the sattvic qualities. Discontent, distress, grief, greed and forbearance —
these marks of rajas are seen through bodily causes. Dishonour, delusion, negligence, sleep and drowsiness
arise somehow — the various tamasic qualities. Fault-finding of many kinds, prayer, doubt:
whose mind is well governed is happy here and hereafter. The difference between sattva and the knower of the field, which are subtle:
one creates qualities, the other does not create qualities. As a mosquito and a fig, always joined,
are one with the other and yet in union, separate by nature yet always united;
as fish and water are joined, so are those two. The qualities do not know the Self; he knows the qualities in every way.
The seer of the qualities thinks himself the creator; the senses act to illuminate for the intellect, the best of beings.
While the unwitting, motionless... the Supreme Self, like a lamp-holder, creates the qualities (sattva), and the knower of the field looks on.
This union of sattva and the knower of the field is fixed. There is no support for sattva and for the knower of the field.
Sattva creates the mind, never the qualities. When he rightly restrains their rays by the mind,
then his Self shines like a lamp burning in a pot. The sage who, abandoning natural action, is always delighting in the Self,
and whose self has become the self of all beings, goes to the highest goal. As a water-bird is not wetted by water,
so one of fixed wisdom moves among beings. Thus a man should live by his own nature through his own intellect.
Not grieving, not exulting, equal, free of envy, yoked by the right means, he always creates the qualities.
As a spider spins its thread, the qualities are to be understood as threads. Once destroyed they do not return; no return is found.
What is invisible is established by inference from the visible; thus some decide; others, 'cessation'.
Having considered both, one should decide according to his understanding. This firm knot of the heart, made of intellectual thought,
having released, one should sit happily, not grieving, his doubts cut. The impure attain purity as men do in a full river.
The very learned, having plunged in, know the cutting of knowledge. One who knows the far shore of a great river is not scorched, nor is he who crosses otherwise.
The knower of the truth is not scorched, the knower of the family crosses. Those who thus know the Self, the supreme knowledge of isolation,
thus realizing, every man, the course of beings' coming and going, reflecting slowly with intellect, thereby gains peace.
He who knows the three aims and who, having looked, lets go, seeking with disciplined mind, seeing the truth, free of eagerness,
the Self cannot be seen in the senses separately, in each, released and hard to reach by the unrefined.
By this knowledge one becomes awakened; what else is the mark of the awakened? Knowing it, the wise think themselves to have done what is to be done.
For the knowers there is no fear from it, while for the ignorant there is great fear. Indeed no one has a higher goal, when the quality is, he declares it incomparable.
He who acts without intention burns up what was done before; both are not disagreeable; how then can they be agreeable, produced by one acting here?
People envy the world and its life; here, doing it, produces it. There see the skilled one not grieve, if fear arises, always in place.
Bharadvaja said: "Teach me the yoga of meditation for the attainment of that state, knowing which, O Brahmin, a man is freed from the threefold affliction."
Bhrigu said: "I shall tell you the fourfold yoga of knowledge, knowing which great sages here attain eternal success.
As meditation is well practised, so yogis do; great sages satisfied with knowledge, their minds gone to nirvana,
are freed from the faults of samsara and do not return; the faults of birth exhausted, they abide in their own nature,
beyond dualities, ever in sattva, freed, without possessions; unattached ways that bring the mind peace.
There one should hold the mind, troubled by meditation, to one point; gathering the host of senses, the sage sits like a log.
He should not know sound by ear, nor feel touch by skin, nor know form by eye, nor tastes by tongue;
the knower of truth should abandon all smells too by meditation. The strong should not desire these that agitate the five groups.
Then, the wise one, having gathered the five groups in the mind, should concentrate the straying mind with the five senses.
Wandering, supportless, with five doors, strong and weak — the steady one should quickly concentrate the mind on the earlier path of meditation.
When he gathers senses and mind together, this is the earlier path of meditation, described by me.
For him, held in that earlier way, the self together with the sixth will flash, as lightning in a cloud, bounded by the sea.
As a trembling drop of water on a leaf moves everywhere, so his mind is on the path of meditation.
Concentrated, it stays a moment on the path of meditation; again the mind wanders the path of wind, like wind.
Undismayed, free of trouble, free of drowsiness and envy, the knower of meditation-yoga should concentrate the mind again by meditation.
Reflection, reasoning and discrimination arise for the sage in samadhi: the first meditation at the start.
Though troubled by the mind, he should bring about concentration; the sage should not lose heart, but do what is good for himself.
As heaps of dust, ashes and dung, suddenly sprinkled with water, do not become pervaded...
but as a little moistened, dry powder untreated gradually becomes wholly pervaded;
so one should slowly bring the host of senses to peace; he should withdraw in order, and it will be well quieted.
In this way the mind and the five groups, O lord of sages, placed first on the path of meditation, are quieted by constant yoga.
Not by human effort nor by anything of fate will happiness come to him who is thus restrained of self.
Joined with that happiness, he will delight in the work of meditation. Thus yogis go to faultless nirvana.
Sanandana said: Thus addressed by Bhrigu, O Brahmin, the mighty Bharadvaja, of supreme dharma, astonished, honoured Bhrigu in return.
This, O wise one, is the origin of the world, fully declared. O greatly wise one, what more do you wish to hear?
See this, O best of Brahmins: all would end in destruction. What difference will it make whether one is careful or careless?
Non-association with beings, or association with perishables — for whom is it done? What is the certain truth here?
Sanandana said: As if with the mind darkened by tamas, the umbrella of intelligence confused, the poet Panchashikha again calmed him with words.
Panchashikha said: "There is no end by annihilation here, nor does a fixed state exist. This aggregate of body, senses and mind
acts separately, yet depending on one another in actions. The elements are fivefold: water, wind in space, light, and earth."
